tiles.title: Inject a controlled failure and verify alarm behavior

blocks.text: Configuration alone does not demonstrate behavior under disruption. Before the approved sandbox fault, define its limited scope, expected signals and abort conditions. During the fault, inspect alarm state history and actual notification receipt. Then remove the fault and verify recovery.

blocks.text: Keep the sandbox record in order: approved limits, fault, alarm behavior, notification receipt, then recovery. An absent notification is a result to preserve, not a successful test inferred from configuration.

If an abort condition is reached, follow the approved stop path. Do not extend the fault to obtain a desired alarm. Retain missed signals, absent notifications and unsuccessful recovery honestly; this exercise does not authorize production disruption.

blocks.text: A published Lambda version freezes function code and most configuration. The alias is movable: it selects a published version for invocations. Use aws lambda publish-version --function-name NAME, then aws lambda update-alias --function-name NAME --name ALIAS --function-version VERSION. Test NAME:ALIAS. For rollback, point the alias at the approved previous version and repeat verification.

tiles.title: Reconcile Terraform EC2 drift; directly require the native EC2 instance foundation

blocks.text: Terraform normally refreshes tracked resources before planning, exposing relevant out-of-band changes. Compare observed EC2 settings with configuration and choose an approved intent: restore the declaration or update it. Inspect a new plan, follow the approval/apply workflow, and verify live settings. Refresh-only planning proposes state and output updates; planning does not persist them. Applying the approved refresh-only plan persists those updates without restoring remote infrastructure to configuration.

tiles.title: Rightsize a resource using a supplied workload baseline

blocks.text: Rightsizing matches resource type and size to workload performance and capacity requirements, not simply the smallest instance. Compare supplied load, utilization and performance with service constraints. Recommend a smaller instance only if those constraints remain satisfied. Include peak and changing demand; one low-utilization sample is not enough.

blocks.caption: EC2 sizing: baseline and candidate evidence

blocks.text: Compare the current size and smaller candidate across normal, peak and changing demand. Keep observed load, measured utilization and latency separate from the recommendation they support.

The current peak reaches the supplied latency boundary. The smaller candidate’s peak and changing-demand latency exceed the supplied bound, so the normal sample cannot justify that reduction. Preserve the constraints and withhold the unsupported reduction; do not invent a price comparison.

The task definition supplies what runs; the service maintains how many tasks are requested. Observe the controlled task loss, replacement progress and restored running count. Keep service events and running/pending counts in the record rather than assuming service creation proves replacement.
